title: Who disciplines whom
ask: Who disciplines a sitting Justice, a lower-court judge, a court employee and a lawyer?
items: Sitting SC Justice: impeachment only (In re Gonzalez)
Retired Justice: the Court, administratively (Biraogo)
Lower-court judges and CA Justices: the Supreme Court en banc (Sec. 11)
Court employees: the Supreme Court through the OCA; the CSC only files (Andal)
Lawyers: the Supreme Court (Gadon)
src: Art. VIII, Secs. 6 and 11; Art. XI, Sec. 2

title: What Maceda v. Vasquez held
ask: State the holdings of Maceda v. Vasquez (1993).
items: The SC has exclusive administrative supervision over all courts and personnel (Sec. 6)
One act may bring administrative and criminal liability
The Ombudsman has jurisdiction over the crime
But a criminal complaint arising from court duties must be referred to the Court first
The Court decides whether the respondent acted within his administrative duties
The Ombudsman cannot compel the Court to produce records or its personnel to testify

title: What CSC v. Andal held
ask: State the holdings of CSC v. Andal (2009).
items: Only the SC oversees court personnel’s compliance with all laws, rules and regulations
The CSC cannot try and decide administrative cases against court personnel
Not even for civil service exam anomalies
The CSC files its complaint with the OCA (Ampong)
No estoppel: he denied the charge, never appeared, and raised jurisdiction on appeal

title: Judges disciplined: the cases
ask: Give the cases where the Court disciplined Justices of the CA or the Court itself, with the penalty.
items: In re Demetria (2001): CA Justice who lobbied prosecutors, dismissed
Re: Vasquez (2008): Roxas dismissed; Sabio suspended two months; Reyes reprimanded; Dimaranan-Vidal admonished; Vasquez severely reprimanded
In re Biraogo (2009): retired Justice Reyes fined ₱500,000 and disqualified for a leaked ponencia
src: Art. VIII, Sec. 6; Code of Judicial Conduct

title: What In re Gadon held
ask: State the holdings of In re Gadon (2023).
items: No inhibition: bias needs clear and convincing proof; the Court acts as a collegial body
Baseless bias claims are direct contempt
Disbarment is sui generis: a fitness inquiry
Preventive suspension may come before the answer when the act speaks for itself
A lawyer cannot divide his personality: private conduct counts
Scandalous, misogynistic speech violates CPRA Canon II; disbarred

title: Change of venue: the rule and the cases
ask: When will the Court change the venue of a trial? Give the cases.
items: Art. VIII, Sec. 5(4): to avoid a miscarriage of justice
Not for whimsical or flimsy reasons; crimes are best tried where committed
Serious and weighty reasons to doubt a fair and impartial trial (People v. Gutierrez)
Pilotin: hostile sentiment endangering the accused’s life
Mondiguing: a judge tied to the victim; danger to the accused
Sola: the effect of fear on the witnesses; doubts favor the change
It may be sought administratively, and moves the whole record
src: Art. VIII, Sec. 5(4); Pilotin; Mondiguing; Sola

title: The SC’s administrative powers in Sec. 5 and 6
ask: List the Supreme Court’s administrative powers under Article VIII.
items: Administrative supervision over all courts and personnel (Sec. 6)
Temporary assignment of lower-court judges, at most six months without consent (Sec. 5(3))
Change of venue or place of trial (Sec. 5(4))
Appointment of all Judiciary officials and employees under the Civil Service Law (Sec. 5(6))
Discipline and dismissal of lower-court judges (Sec. 11)

title: The three writs under Sec. 5(5)
ask: Name the writs the Court created under its power over constitutional rights, with what each covers.
items: Amparo (2007): extralegal killings and enforced disappearances, or threats of them
Habeas data (2008): unlawful gathering, keeping or use of data threatening privacy in life, liberty or security
Kalikasan (2010): environmental damage prejudicing life, health or property in two or more cities or provinces

title: Amparo: the working rules
ask: State the working rules of the writ of amparo.
items: Summary; substantial evidence
Finds responsibility and accountability, not liability
Two stages: writ on a prima facie case; privilege after return and hearing
Totality of evidence; hearsay if consistent (Razon v. Tagitis)
Public officials must prove extraordinary diligence; no presumption of regularity
Command responsibility only to find who must act (Rodriguez)
Red-tagging and surveillance are threats (Deduro; Bautista)
Not for custody disputes (Caram) or contempt detention (Agcaoili)
src: Rule on the Writ of Amparo; Rodriguez; Bautista; Deduro; Caram

title: Enforced disappearance: the elements
ask: Give the elements of enforced disappearance.
items: Arrest, detention, abduction or any deprivation of liberty
By agents of the State, or with its authorization, support or acquiescence
Followed by a refusal to acknowledge it, or concealment of the fate or whereabouts
Placing the person outside the protection of the law
src: RA 10353, Sec. 3(b); Navia v. Pardico; Caram v. Segui

title: RA 10353 (2012): key provisions
ask: List the key provisions of the Anti-Enforced or Involuntary Disappearance Act.
items: The right is non-derogable, even in war or emergency (Sec. 4)
An order of battle is no defense; it may be disobeyed (Sec. 5)
Absolute right of detainees to communicate (Sec. 6)
Duty to certify presence or absence; detention register (Secs. 8, 10)
Priority for habeas corpus, amparo and habeas data (Sec. 12)
Commanding officer liable as principal (Sec. 14)
Reclusion perpetua (Sec. 15)
Continuing offense; no prescription unless the victim surfaces (Secs. 21–22)
No amnesty (Sec. 23)

title: Writ of kalikasan: the elements
ask: What must a petitioner prove for a writ of kalikasan?
items: An actual or threatened violation of the right to a balanced and healthful ecology
Arising from an unlawful act or omission of a public official or a private party
Damage prejudicing life, health or property in two or more cities or provinces
The magnitude of the damage is indispensable
The precautionary principle applies only to an uncertain causal link, not to no evidence
src: RPEC, Rule 7; Water for All Refund Movement v. MWSS (2023)

title: Pimentel v. LEB: what fell and what stood
ask: Which parts of RA 7662 and the LEB’s rules did Pimentel v. LEB strike down, and which survived?
items: Stood: the LEB and RA 7662; legal education is an executive function
Stood: minimum standards for law school admission (Sec. 7(e))
Void: training members of the legal profession (Sec. 3(a)(2))
Void: internship as a requirement for the bar (Sec. 7(g))
Void: mandatory CLE for lawyers (Secs. 2 and 7(h))
Void: the PhiLSAT as a pass-or-fail gate (academic freedom)
hook: Students: the State. Lawyers: the Court.

title: Admission and discipline of lawyers: the cases
ask: Give the admission and discipline cases with their rule.
items: Zaldivar (1988): attacks on the Court’s integrity are misconduct; suspended indefinitely
Aguirre v. Rana (2003): practicing before signing the Roll; admission denied
Garrido (2010): pre-bar bigamy; both lawyers disbarred
In re Ong (2014): Sandiganbayan Justice dismissed for dealings with Napoles
Zoleta (2015): a judge of doubtful citizenship is at least a de facto officer

title: The integrated bar: the cases
ask: Give the three integrated bar cases and their holdings.
items: In re Edillon (1978): compulsory membership and dues valid; stricken from the Roll for not paying
In re 1989 IBP Elections: the Court may suspend oaths, investigate and annul; IBP elections are non-political
Re: Divina (2024): no election offense without a link to an election, but lavish gifts are simple misconduct (₱100,000 fines)
src: Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5); IBP By-Laws, Sec. 14
